question:
Client: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi. Matter: motor accident claim, death of spouse.

Her husband was killed in a road accident involving a commercial truck. The truck driver was operating the vehicle without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies the claim, arguing the policy is void because the driver was unlicensed, and that it bears no liability.

Key facts: deceased aged 42; monthly income Rs 35,000; dependants are the wife and two minor children (8 and 12); the truck was a commercial vehicle owned by a transport company; the driver held no valid licence; the insurer contests liability.

Research the corpus and advise on supporting precedents, adverse precedents, and strategy.

args.question: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi's claim for compensation for death of spouse (aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, 3 dependants) in a commercial truck accident where the driver had no valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing the policy is void due to unlicensed driver.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the driver of the tempo did not possess a valid driving licence. The court held the insurer must pay the third-party award and can recover from the owner/driver.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting precedent. It squarely holds that even where the driver had no valid licence at all, the insurer's statutory liability to the third-party claimant remains intact, with only a right of recovery against the insured.
supporting.quote: The Claims Tribunal, therefore, rightly made the Insurance Company liable to pay the compensation and granted it recovery rights.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver lacked an endorsement to drive a commercial vehicle while holding a valid LMV licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: The vehicle was a commercial vehicle (Mahindra Maxi Cab). The driver held an LMV licence but no commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable to the third party.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Supreme Court judgment establishes that even for commercial vehicles, the absence of a proper licence/endorsement does not defeat the third party's right to recover from the insurer. The insurer must pay and can recover from the insured.
supporting.quote: the insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained in the driving licence.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had only an LMV/transport endorsement but was driving a heavy goods vehicle. The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck where the driver had no licence at all — a stronger case for third-party protection.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Madras High Court judgment applies the Swaran Singh and S. Iyyapan principles to heavy goods vehicles, confirming that the pay-and-recover remedy is available even for class-of-vehicle licence deficiencies.
supporting.quote: the insurer cannot disown its liability... In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation to drive a transport vehicle, the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and then recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had only an LMV licence and no badge/authorisation for a transport vehicle. The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck with no licence at all.
supporting.why_it_matters: This judgment explicitly recognises the 'pay and recover' doctrine for licence deficiencies in transport/commercial vehicles, directly supporting the client's right to receive compensation from the insurer.
supporting.quote: The doctrine of 'pay and recover' has been recognised by the Supreme Court in Several decisions.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant first and then recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all. The tribunal held this was a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest factual match — the driver had no licence whatsoever. Despite finding a fundamental breach, the tribunal protected the third party by ordering pay-and-recover. This directly counters the insurer's argument that 'no licence = no liability.'
supporting.quote: it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired (or absent) driving licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired (effectively no valid licence on the date). The court held the insurer liable to the third party.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the principle that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 is not defeated by licence deficiencies.
supporting.quote: the insurer who is made statutorily liable to pay compensation to third parties on account of the certificate of insurance issued shall be entitled to recover from the insured the amount paid to the third parties, if there was any breach of policy conditions

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: Multiplier must be based on deceased's age; future prospects apply to self-employed persons at 25% for age 40-50; 1/3 deduction for 3 dependants.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 42 (within 40-50 bracket), self-employed or fixed salary, 3 dependants. The court applied Pranay Sethi principles exactly matching our client's facts.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the authoritative framework for computing compensation: multiplier of 14 (age 42), future prospects at 25%, 1/3 deduction for personal expenses, and conventional heads as per Pranay Sethi.
supporting.quote: In case the deceased was self-employed or on a fixed salary, an addition of 25% where the deceased was between the age of 40 to 50 years... The selection of multiplier shall be as indicated in the Table in Sarla Verma... The age of the deceased should be the basis for applying the multiplier.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks and does not extend to own-damage claims or disputes between insurer and insured where no third party is involved.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach is limited to third-party claims. However, this case actually HELPS the client because it expressly affirms (at point 3 of the holding) that 'In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.' The risk is low because the insurer cannot use this to defeat a third-party claim — it only limits Swaran Singh's application to non-third-party contexts.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment expressly states that for third-party risks (which is our case), the insurer must indemnify and can recover from the insured. It is not adverse — it actually confirms the client's position. The insurer cannot use it to avoid liability because the holding explicitly preserves the pay-and-recover principle for third-party claims.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: Where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the policy terms (gratuitous passengers in goods vehicle), the Tribunal has no power under Section 149(4)/(5) to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may argue by analogy that if the driver had no licence at all, the risk was never one the insurer agreed to cover, and therefore pay-and-recover should not apply. However, this case is about gratuitous passengers — a fundamentally different issue.
